span: Under Section 34(2-A) of the Arbitration Act, a domestic award may be set aside if the Court finds that it is vitiated by ‘patent illegality’ appearing on the face of the award.
why: States the patent-illegality ground; does not itself say whether a mere erroneous interpretation of a contract suffices (the next paragraph discusses interpretation).

span: interprets a clause in the contract which no fair-minded or reasonable person would
why: Headnote holding: courts do not sit in appeal and interfere only for patent illegality, which includes an interpretation no reasonable person would adopt; an ordinary erroneous interpretation is not enough.

span: Provided that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of the law or by reappreciation of evidence.
why: Quoted statutory proviso; the court's own remarks concern which awards may use the patent-illegality plea.

span: an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of the law or by reappreciation of evidence
why: Headnote holding: erroneous application of law is not by itself a ground; only illegality going to the root, or perversity, justifies setting aside.

span: The scope of enquiry in the proceedings under Section 34 of the Act is restricted to a consideration whether any of the grounds mentioned in Section 34(2) or Section 13(5) or Section 16(6) are made out
why: Says s.34 inquiry is confined to the listed grounds; it does not address erroneous interpretation specifically.

span: Sub-section (2) to Section 34 of the A&C Act stipulates seven grounds on which a court may set aside an arbitral award.
why: Descriptive survey of the s.34(2) grounds before analysing the case law.
